gap: No result ChatGPT got states that leaving the inverter on all weekend uses up the margin for the second charge: reviewers measured idle draw of about 27 W on the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max (The Solar Lab), 10 W on the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 (The Gadgeteer) and a little over 10% of the battery per 24 h on the Anker SOLIX S2000 (Notebookcheck). Over 48 h that is roughly 1,300 Wh, 480 Wh and 400 Wh, against about 250 Wh of margin left after two 700 Wh charges. Separately, ChatGPT's own catalog card showed the S2000, which is lighter and cheaper than the cited pick, at 16.2 kg and $699.99.
standout_why: I compared against the pages ChatGPT got or cited. powerstationgearlab.com (cited) says 'We haven't run these units ourselves'. It plans on about 70% of rated capacity and gives no idle draw or measured usable Wh. powerbencher.com tested nothing, lists no prices and assumes a 15% loss. Neither page mentions inverter standby draw over a multi-day trip. ChatGPT's two answers use only label Wh times an efficiency factor, and none of the results has a measured idle or usable figure for the Elite 200 V2, the DELTA 3 Max or the S2000.
decides: Two 700 Wh charges need about 1,650 Wh at the AC outlet (1,400 / 0.85, using powerbencher's 15% loss allowance). The 2 kWh class clears that by only about 250 Wh: 1,910 Wh measured on the Elite 200 V2 and just over 1,900 Wh on the S2000. So the second charge works only if the AC inverter is switched off (or ECO mode used) between charges. With the inverter left on, the DELTA 3 Max loses about 650 Wh a day and drops to roughly one charge, which makes it the clear loser. The Elite 300 at $1,199 (3,014 Wh) is the only priced pick with enough headroom to leave the AC on. On price per Wh and weight, the Anker SOLIX S2000 beats the Elite 200 V2 ($699.99 vs $899, 16.2 kg vs 24.2 kg, similar measured usable Wh). It loses only on availability, with Anker quoting 'Ship within 2-3 weeks', so the Elite 200 V2 is the pick for a trip this month and the S2000 is the value pick if the trip is later.

Same reviewer reports usable capacity 'within ~2000Wh of capacity (>93%)'.

findings.label: Idle draw, AC on, nothing connected
findings.value: just over 10% of battery per 24 h (≈200 Wh/day, ≈8.4 W)
findings.source_title: Anker Solix S2000 power station review (Notebookcheck)
findings.note: Quote: 'It uses only just over 10 percent of its battery charge per 24 hours when left switched on with AC enabled.' 10% × 2,010 Wh ≈ 200 Wh/day, so ≈ 400 Wh over 48 h: 1,900 − 400 ≈ 1,500 Wh, below the ~1,650 Wh needed. About 3 W in UPS bypass mode.

findings.label: Idle draw, AC inverter on, nothing plugged in
findings.source_title: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Review: A Step Forward or a Step Sideways? (The Solar Lab)
findings.note: The Solar Lab: idle 'about 27 watts', which the reviewer says would drain the unit in 'roughly three days'. It reports 79% overall efficiency (method not stated), weight 45 lb, and no measured usable Wh. 27 W × 48 h ≈ 1,300 Wh, so leaving the inverter on over a weekend costs more than one full e-bike charge. Page shows no author or date.

findings.label: AC energy needed for two 700 Wh charges
findings.value: ≈1,650 Wh at the station's AC outlet
findings.source_title: Best Portable Power Stations for E-Bikes and Scooters (2026) (powerbencher)
findings.note: 1,400 Wh / 0.85 using powerbencher's assumed ~15% inverter+charger loss allowance (not measured). The station's measured usable output (~1,900–1,910 Wh) is already net of inverter loss, so applying the full 15% here is conservative. The margin is still about 250 Wh, which a weekend of inverter idle uses up on every 2 kWh model.
